catalog_quote: The loudest and most noticeable syllable of a word is called the stressed syllable of the word. Stress in Yapese is not well-understood. Words ending in a syllable with a long vowel, followed by a syllable with a short vowel are stressed on the long vowel. An example is sáalap ‘expert’, where the accent mark is placed over the stressed syllable. ... Words ending in a long vowel, such as deengkii ‘electricity’, are stressed on the syllable before the final long vowel. Thus déengkii is stressed, as indicated, on the first syllable. Other words in Yapese are stressed on the last syllable of the word. These words all have stress on the last syllable of the word, as indicated by the acute accent mark: chibiy ‘to lift’ paqág ‘my hand’ moeróes ‘savage’ ... m'agpáaq ‘wedding’ rogón ‘its way’ ... audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held OA reissue of Jensen 1977 at the stated section and pages (2.5.4.15, pp. 99-100, PDF p. 120-121). Jensen 1977 is the standard reference grammar and, per Dougherty 2024's literature review (pp. 6-7) and his own stress section (pp. 51-53, which simply restates Jensen citing Jensen 1977a: 99-101 and Lynch 2000: 64), no later primary or instrumental description of Yapese word stress exists; the two acoustic studies of Yapese concern glottalized consonants. Dougherty's 2024 restatement (default final stress; penult when penult long + final short; penult when the final syllable is an open long vowel, loanwords only) matches our the primary-stress rule and the CVV/right-edge weight-hedged coding exactly. sources.quote: 'The stress system in Yapese follows three patterns: a default pattern of final stress and two alternate patterns where weight attracts stress. ... (58) gives an example of the default, ultimate stress pattern ... wechweach. In the first of these alternate patterns, stress falls on the penult when the vowel of the penult is long and the vowel of the ultima is short (Jensen 1977a: 99-101; Lynch 2000: 64) ... saalap [ˈsa:.lap].
